stem.text: Natural selection and artificial selection (selective breeding) both have important roles in evolutionary change.
Seahorses are fish with an unusual appearance and many specialised features.

stem.caption: Fig. 8.1
stem.alt: Photograph of a seahorse with its curved tail and elongated snout.

stem.text: Two species of seahorse, Hippocampus erectus and H. zosterae, are found in the coastal waters of the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea.

items: It is thought that these two species of seahorse have a common ancestor.
The ranges of the two species overlap in many areas.
Male and female seahorses stay together for the whole of the breeding season.
H. erectus is much larger than H. zosterae.
Few seahorses occur that are intermediate in size between the two species.

stem.text: Use this information to name and explain the type of speciation that may have occurred in the evolution of these two species.

points.text:
any two from:
no geographical barrier / not geographically isolated ;

explanation.text: Overlap in range removes a present geographical separation as the main explanation. Pair formation and size differences can restrict interbreeding within the same area, allowing reproductive isolation to develop.

reasoningChain: Identify the evidence about geographical range.
Relate the stated breeding features to isolation.
Name the speciation route consistent with that evidence.

stem.text: For many years, farmers have used selective breeding to improve the milk yield of dairy cattle and to improve the yield of crops.
Explain why improving milk yields in cattle by selective breeding can be more challenging than improving yields of crops by selective breeding.

markScheme.instruction:
any three from:
ora in terms of easier for crop yields

points.text: feature can only be measured in, about 50% of offspring / females ;
milk yield must be measured over period of time ;
ref. to difficulty in identifying suitable males for use in crosses ;

cattle require more, care / support
or
more expensive ;
AVP ; e.g. more dangerous to carry out breeding of large cattle

explanation.text: Consider how quickly selection can be repeated and how accurately breeding value can be assessed. Long generations, few offspring and a trait measured only in lactating females all restrict the rate at which useful evidence is obtained.

reasoningChain: Compare generation time and family size.
Consider which offspring express the measured trait.
Relate management requirements to repeated selection.

stem.text: State two examples of crop features that may be improved by selective breeding to increase the yield of crops.

points.text: AVP ; e.g. resistance to, flooding / wind

explanation.text: A yield improvement may come from producing more harvestable material or losing less of it to disease, pests or environmental stress. Name a selectable crop feature rather than a genetic-engineering procedure.

reasoningChain: Identify a feature affecting harvestable yield.

bullets: Stronger candidates noticed that there was no geographical barrier between the two species in this example and correctly identified and explained how sympatric speciation may have occurred. Weaker candidates often did not engage with the information provided and assumed that allopatric speciation was occurring.

This question, directly assessing a syllabus Learning Outcome, was not well answered by the majority of candidates. Few considered, in comparison with crops, the longer time needed for cattle to become sexually mature, the smaller number of offspring that can be produced in each cross or that milk yield can only be determined in half the offspring. Issues relating to the husbandry of large mammals were considered by very few candidates.
Most candidates were able to give two features that would help to increase the yield in crops.
